title: Argus

jokes.text: It is a Vietnamese size two.
jokes.setup: Liz mentions she just got her bridesmaid's dress for Cerie's wedding.
jokes.punchline: It's a 'Vietnamese size two' — implying it's comically small and she can't fit into it.
jokes.explanation: Efficient, specific punchline that does double work: establishes the dress subplot and gets a laugh at Liz's body-image anxiety, which is deeply character-specific. 'Vietnamese size two' is a precise, unexpected qualifier that elevates it above a generic 'the dress is too small' complaint.

jokes.text: Do you know what it's like when a younger man shows up wearing the same cufflinks? You might as well be invisible.
jokes.setup: Liz complains that dressing up is hard for her. Jack responds as if commiserating.
jokes.punchline: Jack's version of a 'dressing up' problem is a cufflink rivalry with a younger man — a completely tone-deaf, aristocratic non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jack Donaghy move: appearing to relate to Liz while revealing a completely alien world of privilege. 'You might as well be invisible' is the perfect deadpan cap — he's treating a cufflink clash as social annihilation. Strong character integration; only Jack could deliver this with a straight face.

jokes.text: A suicide cult! / A gym.
jokes.setup: Liz says she has a plan and joined something 'this morning.'
jokes.punchline: Jack immediately assumes 'A suicide cult!' while Liz's actual answer is 'A gym.' The gap between Jack's assumption and reality is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A textbook simultaneous-speak joke executed with perfect timing. The comedy comes from the absurd distance between Jack's guess (suicide cult) and Liz's reality (gym), but also from Jack's utter lack of alarm at the prospect. Two words, maximum impact — exemplary economy. Rewatch bonus because you anticipate it differently knowing where it lands.

jokes.text: If the will says that you have to spend the night in a haunted house, you better hope that everybody else there is black guys and sluts.
jokes.setup: Jack says he was named in Don Geiss's will and this is a difficult time.
jokes.punchline: Liz subverts the condolence moment with a horror-movie survival-strategy joke.
jokes.explanation: A sharp, politically incorrect riff on horror movie tropes that's unexpected in this context. It's funny because it's Liz's idea of empathy — practical, pop-culture-drenched advice instead of emotional support. Slightly cheap in its reliance on a familiar observation, but the deployment is clever.

jokes.text: Maybe that boyhood sled he held so dear. I believe he called it... Sleddy.
jokes.setup: Jack lists mundane items he wants from the will (pen, tie clip), building toward something meaningful.
jokes.punchline: 'Sleddy' — a Citizen Kane/Rosebud parody delivered with absolute sincerity and the hilariously banal name.
jokes.explanation: A brilliant, economical Citizen Kane parody that works on multiple levels: the grandiose setup ('boyhood sled he held so dear'), the dramatic pause, and the completely deflating punchline of 'Sleddy.' Jack's absolute earnestness makes it land harder. High originality for how seamlessly a classic film reference is compressed into one word. One of the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: Something which I, in turn, can then pass on to my... Protege. Any chance it's one of those bendy hospital beds? Maybe. He did have three.
jokes.setup: Jack speaks sentimentally about passing something on to his protege. Liz, characteristically crass, asks if it might be a hospital bed.
jokes.punchline: Jack confirms Don had three bendy hospital beds — an unexpectedly specific and absurd detail that reveals Don Geiss's extravagant eccentricity in death.
jokes.explanation: The joke has two beats: Liz's crass pivot and Jack's deadpan confirmation with the escalating detail of 'three.' 'Three' is the magic comedy number used perfectly here — it implies Don's indulgent, mysterious lifestyle without over-explaining.

jokes.text: Life is like TV. Testing tells us that people like weddings, births, and episodes where a character dies. That's dumb. My heart!
jokes.setup: Jack makes a meta-comment about TV tropes, Liz calls it dumb.
jokes.punchline: Tracy immediately fakes a heart attack — performing the exact cheap emotional manipulation Jack just described.
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly constructed meta joke: Jack describes a TV cliché, Liz dismisses it, and Tracy immediately enacts a different cliché ('My heart!') — the show eating itself. The meta-awareness is layered and the callback structure is executed in under five seconds. Exceptional structure.

jokes.text: You sound like my mother talking to the planned parenthood lady.
jokes.setup: Grizz says 'Um, I haven't decided yet' about his best man.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's non-sequitur comparison to his mother at Planned Parenthood — absurdly specific and darkly comic.
jokes.explanation: Classic Tracy absurdism: using a deeply personal, darkly specific family memory as a random comparison. The specificity ('planned parenthood lady') is what makes it work — it implies a whole tragic backstory while being played purely for comedy. Very Tracy-specific.

jokes.text: Which one of your rich and famous friends with hepatitis B are you going to pick?
jokes.setup: Tracy presses Grizz about choosing a best man from his famous friends.
jokes.punchline: 'With hepatitis B' — a casual, specific medical detail added as if it's simply a known fact about celebrities.
jokes.explanation: A funny aside that works because Tracy treats hepatitis B as a standard celebrity trait. It's a bit throwaway but still lands with Tracy's characteristic confidence.

jokes.text: You sound like my mother being pulled onstage at a 2 Live Crew concert.
jokes.setup: Grizz says 'Let's not do this in front of everybody.' Tracy echoes it back mockingly.
jokes.punchline: Tracy escalates from the Planned Parenthood joke to an even more specific, outrageous memory of his mother at a 2 Live Crew concert.
jokes.explanation: A perfect escalation of the running Tracy's-mother gag. The specificity of '2 Live Crew concert' is hilarious, and the image of a reluctant woman being pulled onstage at an explicitly sexual rap concert is perfectly absurd. Tracy's tagline 'My mother had problems' delivers the capper with devastating deadpan. One of the episode's standout moments.

jokes.text: Damn. My mother had problems.
jokes.setup: Tracy has just compared his mother to a woman pulled onstage at a 2 Live Crew concert.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's calm, sad acknowledgment: 'My mother had problems.' Understatement as the punchline.
jokes.explanation: Four words that function as the perfect comedic landing pad after an escalating absurd flight. The understatement — 'problems' — is doing enormous work. The pause implied before it and the matter-of-fact delivery make this a memorable, quotable moment. Near-perfect economy.

jokes.text: Oh, brother, we have to tell Jenna we can't do her Kardashian sketch because Jack is 'bros' with Lamar Odom.
jokes.setup: Scene transition; Liz walks up to Pete.
jokes.punchline: The implication that Jack's bro-network with NBA players blocks sketch comedy content — absurd celebrity networking as a production obstacle.
jokes.explanation: A functional world-building joke that reveals Jack's absurd social connections and how they affect TGS. 'Bros' with Lamar Odom is funny for the specificity, but it's more of a setup for how the show operates than a fully developed joke.

jokes.text: Are you soaking your tampon in vodka again?
jokes.setup: Pete notices Jenna is oddly happy and asks why she's being 'so happy and nice.'
jokes.punchline: Pete's explanation for Jenna's happiness is that she's secretly consuming vodka via tampon — an outrageously specific, gross bit of backstory.
jokes.explanation: The joke functions on multiple levels: it's a real teenage drinking trend being used as a character beat, it implies Pete has seen Jenna do this before (character history), and the word 'again' is the key — treating this as a known recurring behavior. Highly quotable and specific to this world.

jokes.text: Because the glue is abrasive.
jokes.setup: Pete asks if Jenna is soaking her tampon in vodka 'again.' Scene cut to Jenna.
jokes.punchline: Jenna begins mid-sentence explaining why she's NOT doing that — 'because the glue is abrasive' — implying she's tried a variation involving glue.
jokes.explanation: A perfect mid-sentence cut joke. 'Because the glue is abrasive' implies an entire off-screen experiment that the audience has to reconstruct, and the conclusion is horrifying and hilarious. The economy is exceptional — five words do the work of a paragraph. One of the episode's cleverest structural moments.

jokes.text: Is there any chance this might make our lives easier? No way. I have seen this 100 times. She gets psyched about some guy, he reveals himself to be crazy, then there's a terrible breakup, and we suffer.
jokes.setup: Jenna announces a new boyfriend. Liz asks Pete if this could be a good thing.
jokes.punchline: Pete has a systematic, experienced breakdown of the Jenna relationship cycle — framing her love life as a recurring workplace hazard.
jokes.explanation: A solid bit of character-establishing exposition that's also genuinely funny — Pete's world-weary pragmatism about Jenna as a workplace hazard is well-observed. More functional than outstanding.

jokes.text: Remember when she dated that sniper? / And so it's over. Jenna, there's a laser sight on your forehead. / Oh, please. He's not gonna fire. For God's sakes, he's scared of his own mother! Aren't cha, Alan? / Aah!
jokes.setup: Pete recalls a past Jenna relationship disaster as a warning about her new guy.
jokes.punchline: The flashback reveals Jenna was dating a literal sniper, was blasé about a laser sight on her forehead, and then taunted the sniper into firing anyway.
jokes.explanation: An extraordinary cutaway gag that's perfectly constructed. Every line escalates: the casual mention of a sniper boyfriend, the laser sight on Jenna's forehead played as an everyday annoyance, and Jenna psychologically manipulating the sniper by calling out his maternal fear — which immediately backfires. This is premium 30 Rock absurdism: character-specific (only Jenna would do this), escalating, and with a perfect button ('Aah!'). Arguably the funniest single moment in the episode.

jokes.text: Remember this breakup, when she bit me? Pete, that was, like, two years ago. It just won't heal.
jokes.setup: Pete and Liz discuss the danger of Jenna breakups.
jokes.punchline: 'It just won't heal' — Pete was bitten by Jenna two years ago and the wound is still open, played completely straight.
jokes.explanation: The escalating horror of Jenna's relationships continues. The two-year wound is both absurd and a character indictment — Pete just accepts a festering bite wound from his coworker as part of the job. The deadpan delivery of 'it just won't heal' is the key. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: His daughter. His lovely wife. His even lovelier mistress. The secret Canadian family. And his even more secret attic family.
jokes.setup: The estate lawyer reads through the beneficiaries of Don Geiss's will.
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from conventional (daughter, wife) to darkly absurd (mistress → secret Canadian family → 'even more secret attic family'), each level of secrecy more ridiculous.
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in escalating list comedy. The structure is perfect: 'lovely' → 'even lovelier' signals the escalation is coming, and 'attic family' is the perfect absurdist cap — invoking Jane Eyre's mad-wife-in-the-attic imagery while just being its own insane thing. The 'even more secret' modifier is immaculate. One of the episode's best-constructed jokes.

jokes.text: My beloved pet peacock, Argus.
jokes.setup: Jack expects a meaningful, tangible heirloom from his beloved mentor.
jokes.punchline: He receives a live peacock.
jokes.explanation: The episode's central absurd premise delivered with great timing. Works primarily as premise-establishment rather than a self-contained joke, but the gap between Jack's sentimental expectation and a live peacock is a solid comedic premise.

jokes.text: Hello, old friend. [Jack greets the peacock with complete sincerity]
jokes.setup: Jack is presented with the peacock from the will.
jokes.punchline: Jack greets the bird as 'old friend' with genuine gravitas — treating a peacock as a dignified acquaintance.
jokes.explanation: Three words that work entirely because of who's saying them. Jack's complete sincerity and social decorum applied to a peacock is a perfect character beat. Maximum economy.

jokes.text: Ugh! Vietnamese size two. [Liz struggles with the bridesmaid dress — visual gag inferred]
jokes.setup: Earlier Liz mentioned she joined a gym to fit into the dress.
jokes.punchline: The dress problem persists — the gym plan has already failed or is clearly not working, shown visually.
jokes.explanation: A callback that reestablishes the running gag. The repetition of 'Vietnamese size two' works as a callback punchline — we know exactly what she means. Functional running gag beat.

jokes.text: Because of our sexual past. [Cerie asks why it would be awkward; Beth says this]
jokes.setup: Cerie asks Beth why it would be awkward that Tracy brought up her wedding.
jokes.punchline: Beth drops 'Because of our sexual past' — a completely unexpected revelation delivered as if it explains everything.
jokes.explanation: A great blind-side joke — zero setup for a sexual history between these two characters, delivered with maximum confidence. The economy is excellent, and it immediately raises questions about the show's world in a funny way.

jokes.text: Leave it open. I'd feel safer. [After the sexual past revelation, Grizz asks Beth to leave the door open — reaction beat]
jokes.setup: Beth just revealed a sexual past with Cerie as Grizz enters.
jokes.punchline: Grizz, presumably having just heard this or sensing the tension, asks for the door to be left open — implying he's uncomfortable being alone with Beth after that revelation.
jokes.explanation: A quick, funny reaction beat. Grizz's discomfort with Beth after the revelation is played with perfect brevity. The joke lives in his need for an open door as a safety measure.

jokes.text: You know my every thought, Beth. We really were the Sam and Diane of this place.
jokes.setup: Beth correctly anticipates Grizz's predicament about Tracy.
jokes.punchline: Grizz romanticizes their dynamic as 'Sam and Diane' — the iconic TV couple from Cheers — despite this being a professional relationship between a giant NBA player and a page.
jokes.explanation: A solid joke that plays on the absurdity of Grizz casting himself and Beth as a classic TV romantic pair. Works because of the incongruity of the reference applied to these characters.

jokes.text: Through a mutual fund. Friend, Jenna. / Oh, of course. Through a friend fund. Noted.
jokes.setup: Liz asks how Jenna and Paul met.
jokes.punchline: Paul says 'mutual fund' when he means 'mutual friend.' Liz mishears it as 'friend fund' and accepts this nonsense term, writing it down.
jokes.explanation: A tight wordplay joke that also characterizes Liz: she mishears, invents a term ('friend fund'), and immediately accepts it as fact — efficient comedy writing. Also plants suspicion about Paul by introducing him with a nervous slip.

jokes.text: He works for a bankrupt circus.
jokes.setup: Paul says he works for 'a bank.' He's cut off by noise.
jokes.punchline: Pete hears '...rupt circus.' Together they assemble 'bankrupt circus' as Paul's employer — an absurdist, perfect misheard answer.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed misheard-conversation joke where the answer assembled from two partial fragments ('a bank' + 'rupt circus') is more interesting and funnier than either half. 'Bankrupt circus' is also a perfect absurdist job that later proves thematically resonant. Structurally elegant.

jokes.text: I'm guessing... already-married cat strangler.
jokes.setup: Liz says Paul is hiding something based on all the odd behavior.
jokes.punchline: Pete's specific guess: 'already-married cat strangler' — two separate horrifying crimes bundled together as one compound noun.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'cat strangler' next to the more domestic 'already-married' is an odd pairing that works through incongruity. Pete's willingness to jump to a very dark conclusion is character-appropriate.

jokes.text: Agh! Living dinosaur! [Liz's reaction to suddenly encountering the peacock in the hallway]
jokes.setup: Liz is in the hallway; suddenly a peacock appears.
jokes.punchline: Liz screams 'Living dinosaur!' — her panicked, evolutionarily-informed description of a peacock.
jokes.explanation: Liz calling a peacock a 'living dinosaur' is funny because it's technically accurate (birds are avian dinosaurs) but also reveals she's the kind of person who would think like this in a panic. Character-specific and highly quotable.

jokes.text: Peacocks can live up to 40 years, longer if they're not part of Mike Tyson's home zoo.
jokes.setup: Jack explains peacock longevity to Liz.
jokes.punchline: 'Longer if they're not part of Mike Tyson's home zoo' — a real-world reference (Tyson famously kept tigers) applied as a peacock-specific caveat.
jokes.explanation: A great throwaway that works because Tyson's exotic animal hobby is real, making the joke feel rooted. Adding 'home zoo' as a casual detail — as if this is just a known habitat risk — is the key. Jack delivers it as a simple fact, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: How to avoid getting paper cuts while making love on a pile of money.
jokes.setup: Jack describes his idyllic memory of sitting with Don Geiss, discussing 'business, politics...'
jokes.punchline: The list of civilized topics escalates to 'how to avoid paper cuts while making love on a pile of money' — an absurdly specific rich-person problem.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect joke. The setup mimics the rhythm of respectable intellectual discourse ('business, politics...') then pivots to a problem so specific and wealthy that it implies an entire lifestyle. 'Paper cuts' is the key word — it's the mundane detail within the absurd that makes it transcendent. Only Jack could deliver this as a sincere, warm memory. Extremely quotable and one of the episode's peaks.

jokes.text: We three peacocks felt like we owned the world.
jokes.setup: Jack has been describing himself, Don Geiss, and the peacock Argus as companions.
jokes.punchline: Jack unselfconsciously includes himself in the category of 'peacocks' — making it a trio of peacocks, not two men and a bird.
jokes.explanation: Jack identifying himself as a peacock alongside Don and Argus is a beautifully understated moment of absurdity delivered straight. The self-aggrandizing vanity of 'peacock' suits Jack perfectly. The 'three' is also a callback to 'We three kings' carol structure — whether intentional or not, it adds gravitas that makes the joke land harder.

jokes.text: Oh, his feather went in my mouth. Ew, it's so oily. / Lemon, he's marked you. He thinks you're his wife.
jokes.setup: Jack's emotional speech about Don Geiss is interrupted when the peacock puts a feather in Liz's mouth.
jokes.punchline: Jack reframes this as the peacock choosing Liz as a mate — instantly pivoting from grief to peacock marital law.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from a sincere emotional moment to peacock mating behavior is a great tonal whiplash joke. 'He's marked you' has the gravity of a pronouncement. Liz's 'Ew, it's so oily' is the perfect mundane reaction to a grand avian ritual.

jokes.text: Really? I'd be awesome at that. / You would. / Now of course you couldn't sing and-- / But who's gonna tell you two? The wedding band is U2? / No! You two idiots!
jokes.setup: Beth and Grizz try to manipulate Tracy into not being best man by offering him a 'lead singer' role.
jokes.punchline: Tracy mishears 'you two' as 'U2' the band — and the confusion cascades perfectly.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully timed homophone joke. The confusion arises naturally from the setup, and Tracy's excitement about 'U2' being the wedding band is perfect character comedy — of course Tracy assumes a famous band would be involved. The resolution ('You two idiots!') is crisp.

jokes.text: I see what you're trying to do. You're trying to manipulate me into not being the best man. And, damn it, Grizz, I've known you since you was six feet tall!
jokes.setup: Tracy sees through the best man manipulation attempt.
jokes.punchline: 'I've known you since you was six feet tall!' — Tracy's version of a long friendship ('since you were a kid') recalibrated for a giant, implying Grizz was six feet tall as a child.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. Tracy reuses a cliché of long friendship ('since you were small') but recalibrates it for a giant character — implying Grizz was six feet tall as a child. It's character-specific, absurdist, and deeply quotable. The grammatically imperfect 'you was' adds to Tracy's voice authenticity.

jokes.text: I am the leader of this entourage! And because of you, I'm having a tantrum! Now pick up that table and smash it for me!
jokes.setup: Tracy doubles down on his position about being best man.
jokes.punchline: Tracy announces his own tantrum as if it's a bureaucratic procedure, then delegates the physical destruction to someone else.
jokes.explanation: Tracy formally announcing his own tantrum and then outsourcing the physical component is a sublime piece of character comedy. It captures his celebrity ego perfectly: the tantrum is his right, but the table-smashing is labor he can delegate. 'Smash it for me' is the killer phrase. Highly quotable and deeply Tracy-specific.

jokes.text: I'm just feeling the weight of Jenna's jewelry on my finger pads.
jokes.setup: Pete/Liz find Paul doing something suspicious — apparently trying on Jenna's jewelry.
jokes.punchline: Paul's explanation — 'feeling the weight on my finger pads' — is an oddly specific, sensual way to describe trying on jewelry, deepening the mystery of his character.
jokes.explanation: A good mystery-building joke. 'Finger pads' is an oddly precise phrase that suggests Paul has thought about this a lot. Foreshadows his Jenna impersonator reveal without giving it away.

jokes.text: Oklahoma. They couldn't find cowboy hats big enough for my kid's head, so they're just wearing turbans.
jokes.setup: Liz asks if Pete's kids have a play tonight when she wants to stay out following Paul.
jokes.punchline: Pete's kids are performing Oklahoma in turbans because their heads are too big for cowboy hats.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly constructed throwaway about Pete's messy domestic life. The solution (turbans instead of cowboy hats because heads are too big) is both logistically absurd and visually hilarious — a geography-confused production of Oklahoma. Pete's children's abnormally large heads as an established fact is wonderfully weird character background.

jokes.text: Words are the first step on the road to deeds!
jokes.setup: Scene cut to Tracy apparently addressing or motivating himself or someone else.
jokes.punchline: Tracy delivers a bombastic motivational platitude in isolation — context-free, suggesting he was mid-monologue.
jokes.explanation: A short Tracy non-sequitur that works primarily through delivery and context-free confidence. Mildly funny on its own, funnier in the rhythm of the episode.

jokes.text: Oh, my, what a gorgeous swamp eagle.
jokes.setup: Jack presents Argus the peacock to what appears to be a doctor or vet.
jokes.punchline: The vet misidentifies a peacock as a 'swamp eagle' — either absurdly incompetent or being diplomatic.
jokes.explanation: 'Swamp eagle' is a wonderfully specific wrong answer. It implies the vet has a taxonomy of exotic birds in his head but is retrieving the wrong one — or the show is satirizing the eccentricity of Jack's 'crazy rich person's pet store.' Economy is high; the joke lives in those two words.

jokes.text: He lives... or you die.
jokes.setup: Jack tells Kenneth that Argus's welfare is his only concern, stopping all page duties.
jokes.punchline: Jack escalates to a death threat with complete calm — 'He lives or you die' — as if this is a normal management directive.
jokes.explanation: Jack threatening Kenneth's life over a peacock's health, delivered as a routine management instruction, is a perfect Jack moment. The economy ('He lives... or you die') is flawless — five words, maximum menace, zero hesitation. Only Jack Donaghy treats mortality as a KPI.

jokes.text: I was about to suggest the same thing.
jokes.setup: Jack says 'He lives or you die.'
jokes.punchline: Kenneth immediately and cheerfully agrees — as if he was already planning to prioritize the bird's life over his own.
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's chipper agreement to the terms of his potential death is a classic Kenneth joke: his selfless, innocent servitude is played so straight that it becomes deeply funny and faintly disturbing. The immediate, enthusiastic response removes any sense of reluctance. Perfect character integration and maximum economy. One of Kenneth's best moments in the episode.

jokes.text: Whoa, you watch your mouth, before I show you the back of my hand.
jokes.setup: Liz calls Tracy 'dummy' while trying to talk sense about the best man situation.
jokes.punchline: Tracy threatens Liz with 'the back of my hand' — an archaic, melodramatic threat delivered completely sincerely.
jokes.explanation: A mild Tracy moment. The threat is vintage Tracy — more bark than bite — but it's not especially inventive. Works for character continuity.

jokes.text: Show up one time, not lose a ring, keep my shirt on through a dinner? Psh.
jokes.setup: Tracy reveals he actually doesn't want to be best man.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's list of best man duties — 'show up one time, not lose a ring, keep my shirt on through a dinner' — reveals exactly which of these he'd find impossible.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's enumeration of what a best man does — phrased in his own terms — reveals his life experience perfectly. 'Keep my shirt on through a dinner' as a distinct, notable achievement is hilarious because it implies this is a real challenge for him. Deep character integration.

jokes.text: He's in love with Grizz's fiancée... Feyonce! / Oh, your stutter is back. / No, Grizz's fiancée's name is Feyonce. Like Beyoncé with an 'F.'
jokes.setup: Tracy dramatically reveals DotCom is in love with Grizz's 'feyonce' — which sounds like a stuttered 'fiancée.'
jokes.punchline: Liz assumes it's a speech impediment; Tracy reveals it's actually the woman's name — Feyonce, like Beyoncé with an F.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's very best jokes. A multi-layered wordplay gem: the name 'Feyonce' sounds like 'fiancée' (leading to Liz's stutter misread), but it's also a Beyoncé pun with a different first letter. The explanation 'Like Beyoncé with an F' is delivered as if this should make everything clear. Exceptionally original, perfectly structured, and extremely quotable. Becomes iconic within the episode.

jokes.text: You think that's impressive, watch me stand on one foot. [Proceeds to fail]
jokes.setup: Liz says she's impressed that Tracy is using his selfishness for good.
jokes.punchline: Tracy offers to top this by standing on one foot — and immediately can't do it.
jokes.explanation: A quick physical comedy beat that works through Tracy's confident offer and immediate failure. Simple but functional — his inability to stand on one foot undercuts his bravado nicely.

jokes.text: That's a bar. We're gonna have to drink a lot to fit in.
jokes.setup: Pete and Liz have been tailing Paul; they follow him to a location.
jokes.punchline: Pete's deadpan assessment of the bar — 'We're gonna have to drink a lot to fit in' — is delivered with the resignation of a man who has clearly done this before.
jokes.explanation: A mild observational gag. Pete's willingness to drink heavily for investigative purposes is a light character beat. Functional.

jokes.text: Can I get five more beers here? Name's Dallas.
jokes.setup: Pete is undercover at the bar and introduces himself.
jokes.punchline: Pete uses his cover name 'Dallas' while ordering five beers — committing fully to the cover while being obviously out of his depth.
jokes.explanation: A fun bit of Pete characterization — his idea of undercover work involves immediate heavy drinking and casually announcing his alias. The name 'Dallas' as a choice is also funny for its blandness.

jokes.text: Ladies and gentlemen, put your hands together for Miss Jinah Baloney! [Paul is revealed performing as a Jenna drag impersonator]
jokes.setup: Liz and Pete have been tracking Paul's secret, building suspense about what he's hiding.
jokes.punchline: Paul's secret is revealed: he's a drag performer doing a Jenna Maroney impersonation — the 'bankrupt circus' job makes sudden sense.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully set-up reveal. The name 'Jinah Baloney' is a near-phonetic riff on 'Jenna Maroney' that immediately signals the joke before the visual confirms it. The entire Paul investigation subplot pays off here with maximum absurdism. Strong rewatch bonus because all the earlier clues (jewelry, 'bankrupt circus') snap into place. One of the episode's peaks.

jokes.text: * My muffin top is all that / Whole grain, low fat / I know you want a piece of that / But I just want to dance *
jokes.setup: Paul has been revealed as a Jenna Maroney drag impersonator.
jokes.punchline: The 'Muffin Top' song — a recurring 30 Rock gag — is performed by someone impersonating Jenna, layers of meta-comedy stacking.
jokes.explanation: The 'Muffin Top' song as sung by a man impersonating Jenna adds a layer of meta-comedy to an already meta show. If you know the song from prior episodes, the rewatch value is extremely high. Even cold, a drag Jenna performing this ridiculous song is very funny.

jokes.text: I'm Jenna. Naturally. / Jenna's boyfriend is a Jenna Maroney impersonator.
jokes.setup: Paul performs as a Jenna impersonator at the bar.
jokes.punchline: Jenna, who has also arrived at the bar, announces herself as 'I'm Jenna. Naturally' — and Liz summarizes the absurdity for the audience.
jokes.explanation: 'Naturally' is the key word — Jenna at a bar featuring her own impersonator is framed as entirely expected. Liz's deadpan summary ('Jenna's boyfriend is a Jenna Maroney impersonator') functions as a great absurdist thesis statement delivered straight.

jokes.text: I'm gonna need five more cranberry juices over here!
jokes.setup: Liz processes the revelation that Jenna is dating her own impersonator.
jokes.punchline: Liz's reaction to the absurdity is to order more cranberry juice — her version of stress-drinking, probably non-alcoholic, at a gay bar.
jokes.explanation: Liz stress-ordering cranberry juice (vs. alcohol) is a good character beat — her version of coping is both funny and specific to her. The callback echo of Pete ordering beers adds a layer.

jokes.text: Lemon, what is with this food layout? Kenneth says he needs some sumac bark and shrub yellow root to make a poultice for Argus. / How is your thing weirder than mine?
jokes.setup: Liz tries to tell Jack about the Jenna/Paul situation.
jokes.punchline: Jack's peacock problem — involving a poultice of sumac bark and shrub yellow root — is somehow weirder than a man who impersonates Jenna Maroney at a drag bar.
jokes.explanation: Liz's exasperated 'How is your thing weirder than mine?' is a great meta-acknowledgment of the episode's competing absurdist plots. The specificity of 'sumac bark and shrub yellow root' is excellent — Kenneth would absolutely know these things.

jokes.text: I did grieve for Don. As soon as Jack Welch told me, I went through all five stages of grief. / Don is dead. / What? You didn't do anything. / Let me retell it-- in slow motion. Don is dead. [slow-motion emotional performance]
jokes.setup: Liz suggests Jack hasn't grieved for Don. Jack insists he did.
jokes.punchline: Jack's 'grief' consisted of a single sentence delivered with a brief pause — then, challenged, he retells it 'in slow motion' to demonstrate the emotional depth he claims to have shown.
jokes.explanation: A brilliant character joke about Jack's emotional unavailability. His entire 'five stages of grief' was a two-word sentence. His solution to being called out is not deeper emotion but better performance — the slow-motion retell. Only Jack would think slow-motion speech = emotional depth. Exceptional character integration and structure.

jokes.text: What if he rolls over on his back and his cloaca fills with mucous?
jokes.setup: Kenneth reports that Argus is sleeping. Jack asks why Kenneth left him alone.
jokes.punchline: Jack's specific worry — the cloaca filling with mucous — is delivered with the urgency of a genuine crisis and the specificity of someone who has read extensively about peacock anatomy.
jokes.explanation: Jack's deep knowledge of peacock anatomy ('cloaca') as an expression of his obsessive care for Argus is funny because it reveals he's done research. The word 'cloaca' is inherently funny, and 'fills with mucous' adds the right amount of visceral grossness. A very Jack panic.

jokes.text: Well, not New York thin, but--
jokes.setup: Liz says she's 'stretched pretty thin' managing the situation.
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately self-corrects to clarify she's not 'New York thin' — inserting a body image anxiety joke mid-sentence.
jokes.explanation: A wonderful mid-sentence self-interruption that reveals Liz's perpetual body-consciousness. The insertion of 'New York thin' as a specific standard she does not meet, acknowledged parenthetically, is deeply Liz Lemon. Exceptional economy — the joke is done in five words as a subordinate clause.

jokes.text: Sorry -- Mrs. Argus.
jokes.setup: Liz tells Kenneth she's not married to the peacock. Kenneth apologizes.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth corrects himself but still calls her 'Mrs. Argus' — the peacock's wife — as if this is the appropriate formal title.
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's cheerful formality ('Mrs. Argus') as a form of apology is a great Kenneth beat — he's trying to be correct while being completely wrong. The callback to Argus marking Liz gives this resonance.

jokes.text: Oh, no, I'm white. I can't read that word. / 'Friend from the neighborhood. Grizz.'
jokes.setup: Beth reads Grizz's letter aloud. It ends with a word Beth, as a white woman, declines to read.
jokes.punchline: Beth self-censors and substitutes 'friend from the neighborhood' — acknowledging the racial dynamic with surprising self-awareness.
jokes.explanation: A quick meta-racial joke that works because of its honesty — Beth pauses to acknowledge her racial position rather than just reading the word. The substitution phrase is polite and completely inadequate in a funny way.

jokes.text: Well, I lost a toe ring in him, so I'd say a lot.
jokes.setup: Liz asks how much Jenna knows about Paul.
jokes.punchline: Jenna's measure of intimate knowledge of a person is whether you've lost jewelry inside them — a wildly TMI answer delivered with complete casualness.
jokes.explanation: An absolutely extraordinary piece of character comedy. 'I lost a toe ring in him' implies a specific sexual act without describing it, and Jenna using this as a metric for intimate knowledge is horrifying and hilarious in equal measure. Only Jenna would say this, only this casually, and treat it as a perfectly reasonable answer. One of the episode's highest points.

jokes.text: Your judgmental badger face.
jokes.setup: Jenna sees Liz's reaction to the Paul revelation and gets defensive.
jokes.punchline: Jenna names Liz's expression 'the judgmental badger face' — a specific, animal-based insult that becomes a recurring term.
jokes.explanation: 'Judgmental badger face' is a perfect insult — specific, animal, compound, and somehow accurate to how Liz must look. The phrase is extremely quotable and works both as a 30 Rock-world insult and as a genuinely creative piece of language. Jenna naming a facial expression is a great character power move.

jokes.text: Looks like one of us is in trouble. [Kenneth looks at camera/aside — reaction beat as he overhears Jack talking to the peacock]
jokes.setup: Jack is talking to the peacock as if Don Geiss might be inside it.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's aside implies he knows the situation is beyond normal — an underreaction to the very weird thing happening.
jokes.explanation: A mild reaction beat that serves as scene punctuation. Kenneth's understated concern is in character but the joke is mostly contextual.

jokes.text: It's just I've never in all my life heard a peacock say 'sempai and kohai.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth mentions that Argus is making unusual sounds for a peacock.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth matter-of-factly reports that the peacock appears to be saying Japanese words — the supernatural premise is stated as a simple observation.
jokes.explanation: The supernatural revelation that the peacock is saying Don's pet Japanese terms is played completely straight by Kenneth — who, as a character, is possibly supernatural himself. The callback to the Rising Sun/Japan trip gives this extra weight. Kenneth's calm delivery of an impossible statement is perfect 30 Rock deadpan.

jokes.text: Sir, I think there's a lot about this world that we don't understand. Like the afterlife. Or how bread turns into toast.
jokes.setup: Jack asks Kenneth if he believes a human soul could be transferred into an animal.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth equates the mystery of the afterlife with the mystery of how bread becomes toast — presenting them as equivalent unknowns.
jokes.explanation: The single best joke in the episode and one of the great Kenneth lines in 30 Rock history. The joke works on multiple levels: Kenneth's rural theological sincerity, the bathetic drop from 'the afterlife' to 'bread becoming toast,' and the deep characterization it provides — Kenneth genuinely views these as equivalent mysteries. The structure is immaculate: serious setup, appropriate middle ground ('the afterlife'), then the devastating non-sequitur ('how bread turns into toast'). Extremely quotable, deeply character-specific, high originality. Benchmarks against the 9.5 anchor provided.

jokes.text: Hello. / Badger. / It's another badger. / The third badger has taken the bait. / Why is everyone code named badger? / I thought you said you wanted to do it this way. / No, I said I didn't care.
jokes.setup: Liz and Pete are doing CIA-style surveillance of Paul.
jokes.punchline: Their spy operation has everyone code-named 'Badger,' including themselves — because Pete used the same code name for everyone when Liz said she 'didn't care.'
jokes.explanation: A tightly constructed bit of situational comedy. The escalation from one badger to three badgers, and the reveal that Liz's indifference caused the naming problem, is well-paced. Pete naming everyone the same code name because Liz said 'I don't care' is excellent passive-aggressive workplace comedy.

jokes.text: Jenna told me I didn't need to hide from you anymore. / All right, let's cut to the chase. What's your game, friend?
jokes.setup: Paul appears without warning since Jenna has apparently cleared him.
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately interrogates him with 'What's your game, friend?' — her suspicion fully intact despite the social context.
jokes.explanation: A mild Liz Lemon paranoia beat. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: I am the luckiest 'shman' in the world.
jokes.setup: Paul begins to describe himself as the luckiest man.
jokes.punchline: 'Shman' — Paul self-censors mid-word on 'man' to use a gender-neutral term, revealing gender identity complexity with a comedic stutter.
jokes.explanation: A subtle but clever joke about Paul's gender identity being in flux — he starts to say 'man' and self-corrects to something more ambiguous. The portmanteau 'shman' is funny in itself. Good economy; the joke is the stutter.

jokes.text: I'd never tuck my penis again if she asked me.
jokes.setup: Paul defends his love for Jenna against Liz's suspicion about using her for his act.
jokes.punchline: Paul's declaration of love involves 'never tucking his penis again' as the ultimate sacrifice — contextualizing his drag performance practice in the most direct way.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely funny and unexpectedly sweet declaration of love, framed in the most specific terms of Paul's drag life. The offer to stop tucking is presented as his greatest possible sacrifice — a romantic gesture that's both absurd and oddly touching. Very quotable.

jokes.text: All I want to do is spend my days listening to her talk and sing and scream at her cleaning lady on the phone.
jokes.setup: Paul explains what he loves about Jenna
jokes.punchline: His list of romantic attractions ends with 'scream at her cleaning lady on the phone' — presented as endearing rather than alarming
jokes.explanation: The escalating list of Jenna's lovable qualities — 'talk and sing and scream at her cleaning lady on the phone' — is funny because the third item is obviously abusive behavior, but Paul includes it with the same warmth as the other two. Good Jenna characterization.

jokes.text: She finally gets to love herself.
jokes.setup: Paul says he doesn't know what Jenna gets out of dating him.
jokes.punchline: Liz's analysis: Jenna is dating her own impersonator because she is in love with herself — literally.
jokes.explanation: A perfect synthesis joke — Liz's psychological insight into Jenna, delivered as a punchline, is both actually true and absurd simultaneously. The entire Paul/Jenna subplot comes together in one sentence. Exceptional economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Ew, Jenna, why are you grabbing his boobs?
jokes.setup: The sweet Paul/Jenna moment resolves; they embrace.
jokes.punchline: Liz's reaction to what she sees — Jenna grabbing Paul's fake breasts — is delivered with pure Liz disgust.
jokes.explanation: A solid button joke on the Paul/Jenna relationship scene. Liz's grossed-out reaction is well-timed and specific enough to work.

jokes.text: I don't know, Argus. Maybe it's the scotch talking, but I think... there might be a man's soul inside you.
jokes.setup: Jack is alone with Argus, scotch in hand, grief building.
jokes.punchline: Jack drunkenly confides to the peacock that he suspects Don Geiss's soul is inside it — with the same tone he'd use for a business confession.
jokes.explanation: 'Maybe it's the scotch talking' as a preface to this particular theory is a great Jack moment — using a social hedge for a completely unhinged supernatural belief. The restraint of 'might be' is perfect Jack hedging applied to something absurd.

jokes.text: You want a drink. [The peacock appears to nod/react in response to Jack asking for a sign from Don]
jokes.setup: Jack asks Don (via the peacock) to give him a sign if he's in there.
jokes.punchline: The peacock's movement is interpreted by Jack as 'You want a drink' — Don's sign is a request for scotch.
jokes.explanation: A sublime absurdist moment. Jack asks for a supernatural sign; the peacock moves; Jack's interpretation is 'You want a drink' — and he accepts this completely. The joke works because of what it says about both Jack and Don: even in death, their relationship is expressed through scotch. Deeply character-specific and tonally perfect.

jokes.text: And I can do that because of our... sexual past. / Damn, Beth, let it go.
jokes.setup: Beth says she's going to speak frankly to Grizz.
jokes.punchline: Beth again invokes 'our sexual past' as the reason she has this privilege — and Grizz, exhausted, tells her to let it go.
jokes.explanation: A good callback to the 'sexual past' gag. Grizz's exhausted 'Damn, Beth, let it go' is the right reaction — the joke is now about Beth's inability to move past this revelation as much as the revelation itself.

jokes.text: Your wedding day is about you and your bride. So who cares what anyone thinks? Love isn't judgmental. Love is patient. Love is... weird. And sometimes gross.
jokes.setup: Beth gives Grizz heartfelt wedding advice.
jokes.punchline: The speech parodies 'Love is patient, love is kind' but pivots to 'Love is... weird. And sometimes gross' — a sudden deflation of the Biblical reference.
jokes.explanation: A well-structured riff on the Biblical 1 Corinthians love passage. The pivot from 'judgmental... patient' (familiar) to 'weird... and sometimes gross' is perfectly timed. The Paul/Jenna subplot makes 'weird and sometimes gross' land especially hard given context.

jokes.text: So now I am Grizz and Feyonce's Woman of Honor. And he wants me to give the same speech at the Hunts Point Marriott while wearing a dashiki. So you're-- In three weddings in the same day, yeah. You're welcome.
jokes.setup: Beth has solved everyone's wedding problems.
jokes.punchline: Beth's solution has accidentally enrolled her in three weddings on the same day, including one at the Hunts Point Marriott in a dashiki — delivered with exhausted pride.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying escalation button on the wedding subplot. 'Hunts Point Marriott' and 'dashiki' are specific enough to be funny. Beth's 'You're welcome' as a martyred closer is a good character beat.

jokes.text: This is awesome! [Someone, likely Tracy, reacts enthusiastically to 'All By Myself' playing in the background]
jokes.setup: The melancholy 'All By Myself' closing montage plays.
jokes.punchline: An enthusiastic 'This is awesome!' from off-screen breaks the emotional register entirely.
jokes.explanation: A quick tonal counterpoint that disrupts the maudlin ending. Works because of the contrast, not because the exclamation itself is especially clever. Tracy's enthusiasm as a tonal wrecker is very on-brand.

tmdb_overview: Wedding fever hits TGS, leaving Liz to sort out Grizz's dilemma when both Tracy and Dot Com want to be his best man. Jenna's new boyfriend, Paul, raises Liz and Pete's suspicions, while Jack is finally forced to deal with the death of his mentor, Don Geiss, when Geiss leaves him a strange but meaningful inheritance.
insight: Absurdist escalation drives 57 jokes across 42 minutes—peak Season 4 density.
